categories.title: Immigration
categories.description: Legal elements, relief paths, and inadmissibility checklists.

sections.heading: What this element requires
bullets: Statutory eligibility under § 245(a) or § 245(i) is necessary but not sufficient
Favorable exercise of discretion under totality of the circumstances
Positive equities must outweigh adverse factors when adverse facts exist
Explain adverse facts; do not ignore them

sections.heading: Facts that prove it
bullets: Family ties → USC/LPR spouse, children, household dependence
Residence / community → years of presence, school, church, civic roles
Employment / taxes → W-2s, returns, letters from employers
Hardship to relatives → medical, financial, caregiving facts
Rehabilitation / GMC → counseling, clean record since offense, character letters
Adverse history → arrests, fraud concerns, immigration violations (with mitigation)

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
bullets: Treating any single factor as dispositive
Omitting adverse facts that appear on forms or biometrics
Inventing pin cites — use `[CITE NEEDED]` for attorney verification
Leaving `[FACT NEEDED]` gaps unflagged in drafts

sections.heading: Sample language pointers
bullets: Lead with one-sentence case theme
“Totality of the circumstances” framing; weigh equities expressly
Pair each adverse fact with mitigation evidence

sections.heading: What this element requires
bullets: Immigrant visa immediately available (Visa Bulletin / USCIS chart guidance)
Admissible under INA § 212(a), or eligible for and granted a waiver
§ 245(a): inspected and admitted or paroled
§ 245(c) bars (preference categories): unlawful status at filing; failure to maintain status; unauthorized employment; certain VWP/transit/crewman entries
Immediate relatives / VAWA / SIJS: broad exemptions from most § 245(c) bars
§ 245(i): grandfathering via approvable-when-filed petition/labor cert on or before Apr 30, 2001 (+ physical presence Dec 21, 2000 if petition after Jan 14, 1998); I-485 Supp. A + penalty fee

sections.heading: Facts that prove it
bullets: Manner of entry → I-94, passport stamps, parole docs, credible EWI timeline
Status history → visa, COS/EOS, overstay dates, work authorization
Petition history → I-130/I-140/I-360/I-526 or labor cert filing date; approval/priority date
Relationship → marriage/birth certificates; IR vs preference category
§ 245(i) presence → Dec 21, 2000 evidence (school, medical, tax, affidavits)

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
bullets: Assuming admission = inspected entry with false USC claim (not a lawful admission)
Preference beneficiary barred by § 245(c) when IR conversion (e.g., LPR spouse naturalizes) would cure
Triggering § 212(a)(9)(B) by consular departure without provisional waiver analysis
Filing without visa availability / wrong Visa Bulletin chart

sections.heading: Sample language pointers
bullets: State pathway: “§ 245(a) as immediate relative” vs “§ 245(i) grandfathered”
Separate eligibility, admissibility, and discretion into distinct sections

topics.title: AOS filing packet & process checklist
topics.cite: Form I-485 instructions; INA § 245; USCIS filing guidance

sections.heading: What this element requires
bullets: Current form editions + correct filing location/fees
Core: I-485; civil surgeon I-693 (timing strategy — validity rules change; confirm current PM); identity/status docs; translations
Family-based: I-130 (concurrent if eligible) or approval + I-864 package
§ 245(i): I-485 Supp. A + penalty fee + grandfathering proof
Optional concurrent I-765 / I-131 (EAD/AP) when eligible
Biometrics → interview → RFE practice; update address within 10 days

sections.heading: Facts that prove it
bullets: Checklist of forms filed + receipt numbers
Medical exam date / civil surgeon
Financial packet date (may need refresh at interview)
Interview notices / RFE deadlines

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
bullets: Expired medicals due to long pendency
Missing certified translations
Abandonment from missed RFE/interview after address change
Concurrent filing when priority date not current

sections.heading: Sample language pointers
bullets: Maintain a living exhibit/form checklist in the matter
Note what must be updated at interview

topics.title: Affidavit of support (I-864)
topics.cite: INA § 213A; 8 CFR § 213a; Form I-864 / I-864W / I-864A
topics.practiceAreas: Family | AOS | Consular | Public charge interface

sections.heading: What this element requires
bullets: Most family-based immigrants need a sufficient Form I-864 sponsor
Income generally ≥ 125% of Federal Poverty Guidelines (100% for active-duty sponsors of spouse/children — verify current instructions)
Assets may supplement in some cases; household members via I-864A; joint sponsor if needed
Sponsor must be USC/LPR (or certain qualifying sponsors) domiciled in U.S.; enforceable support contract
Exemptions / I-864W in limited categories (e.g., some 40-quarter SSA credit cases, self-petitioning widows/VAWA — confirm current eligibility)

sections.heading: Facts that prove it
bullets: Tax returns / W-2 / pay stubs matching I-864 figures
Household size calculation (including intending immigrants)
Assets docs → ownership, liquidity, valuations if used
Joint sponsor package if primary insufficient
Domicile evidence if sponsor abroad temporarily

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
bullets: Wrong household size → under-income finding
Using outdated poverty guidelines
Missing tax transcripts when returns look inconsistent
Assuming employment-based cases always need I-864 (usually not)

sections.heading: Sample language pointers
bullets: Show poverty guideline year + math in a short table
Flag joint-sponsor need early in strategy memo

topics.title: Extreme hardship (qualifying relative)
topics.cite: INA §§ 212(h), 212(i), 212(a)(9)(B)(v); 9 USCIS-PM B; Matter of Cervantes-Gonzalez

sections.heading: What this element requires
bullets: Qualifying relative: usually USC/LPR spouse or parent (check waiver statute — § 212(h) also allows child/son/daughter in some paths)
Hardship if applicant is refused admission / removed — separation or relocation scenarios
Cumulative weighing — one factor need not alone prove “extreme”
Distinct from ordinary hardship of family separation; must be elevated

sections.heading: Facts that prove it
bullets: Medical → diagnoses, treatment plans, caregiver role, country-of-origin care gaps
Financial → income share, debts, housing, inability to support two households
Family/caregiving → minor children, elderly parents, special-needs dependents
Country conditions → safety, employment, education, language barriers for QR
Emotional/psychological → clinician letters; children’s school/IEP impacts
Length of residence / community ties of QR in the U.S.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
bullets: Arguing applicant’s own hardship as if it were QR hardship
Listing ordinary inconvenience without elevation evidence
Ignoring relocation vs separation theory consistency
No corroboration (medical, school, financial docs)

sections.heading: Sample language pointers
bullets: Label each factor; end with cumulative totality sentence
Address both separation and relocation if facts support either path
Cross-walk exhibits: “See Ex. [letter/medical]”

sections.heading: What this element requires
bullets: Identify exact § 212(a) ground(s) before picking a waiver
Meet statutory qualifying-relative / rehabilitation / equities test for that waiver
Separate application (I-601, I-601A provisional UL presence, or I-212 consent to reapply)
All waivers are discretionary even if extreme hardship is shown

sections.heading: Facts that prove it
bullets: Ground triggered → convictions, misrepresentation facts, UL presence timeline, prior removal
Qualifying relative → status proof + relationship docs
Extreme hardship packet → see `extreme-hardship-factors.md`
Rehabilitation / equities → employment, taxes, community, remorse, counseling
I-601A only → UL presence bar anticipated; no other ground that consulate will find

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
bullets: Seeking waiver for non-waivable grounds (e.g., most false USC claims; drug trafficking; many § 212(a)(9)(C) cases until 10 years abroad + I-212)
Wrong form (I-601 vs I-601A vs I-212)
Filing I-601A when other inadmissibility grounds exist
Skipping discretionary equities after proving hardship

sections.heading: Sample language pointers
bullets: Open with ground + waiver authority cite
Hardship section + discrete discretion section
Flag non-waivable issues for attorney strategy call

sections.heading: What this element requires
bullets: Decide which regime applies: inadmissibility (§ 212) vs deportability (§ 237)
§ 212: seeking admission / many benefits (including AOS) — includes EWI and parolees as “seeking admission”
§ 237: inspected and admitted noncitizens (including many overstays)
Same topic labels (crime, security, public charge) ≠ identical statutory tests
Screen every matter at intake for both benefit eligibility and removal exposure

sections.heading: Facts that prove it
bullets: Entry history → inspected/admitted vs EWI vs parole
Prior orders → removal, expedited removal, in absentia
Criminal record → dispositions, sentences, controlled substances
Fraud / claims → visa lies, I-9 USC claims, document misuse
Status violations → overstay, unauthorized work, COS failures

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
bullets: Applying deportability exceptions (e.g., ≤30g marijuana) to an EWI client who is under § 212
Treating parole as admission
Missing form “yes/no” questions that map to § 212 grounds
Counseling naturalization without criminal/deportability screen

sections.heading: Sample language pointers
bullets: First sentence: “Client is subject to [inadmissibility/deportability] because [entry/admission fact].”
Map each form answer to a specific INA subsection

sections.heading: What this element requires
bullets: § 212(a)(9)(B): UL presence >180 days & <1 year → 3-year bar after departure; ≥1 year → 10-year bar after departure
Bar triggers on departure (and seeking admission) — not while remaining in U.S.
UL presence: overstay; or EWI; or status violation after official determination
Key exceptions (B only): under 18; pending asylum (no unauthorized work); TPS/DED/DACA/deferred action; properly filed AOS; timely nonfrivolous EOS/COS; others per PM
§ 212(a)(9)(C) “permanent bar”: aggregate >1 year UL presence or prior removal, then enter/attempt EWI — generally needs 10 years abroad + I-212; B exceptions do not apply (minors accrue for C)

sections.heading: Facts that prove it
bullets: Timeline → each entry/exit, authorized stay end date, EWI dates
Status determinations → NTA, USCIS denial finding status violation
Exception evidence → age, TPS, pending I-485/I-589, DACA
Prior orders → expedited removal, IJ order, reinstatement risk (§ 241(a)(5))

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
bullets: Advising consular processing without modeling 3/10-year trigger
Assuming minor exception applies to § 212(a)(9)(C)
Confusing unauthorized work start date with UL presence start (often overstay date unless official determination earlier)
Ignoring Arrabally/Yerrabelly / advance parole travel issues — verify current USCIS policy before travel advice

sections.heading: Sample language pointers
bullets: Build a dated UL presence chart
State whether client can remain and adjust vs must depart with I-601A

sections.heading: What this element requires
bullets: Willful misrepresentation of a material fact to procure a visa, admission, or other INA benefit
Materiality: misrepresentation tends to shut off a line of inquiry relevant to eligibility
Timely voluntary retraction may cure in some inspection contexts (narrow; fact-specific)
§ 212(i) waiver: extreme hardship to USC/LPR spouse or parent + discretion

sections.heading: Facts that prove it
bullets: Statement / omission → visa DS-160 answers, border secondary, prior apps
Benefit sought → tourist visa, EAD, AOS, entry
Qualifying relative hardship → see `extreme-hardship-factors.md`
Equities / remorse → corrected statements, consistent later filings

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
bullets: Confusing § 212(a)(6)(C)(i) misrepresentation with false USC claim (ii) — different waiver rules
Assuming “honest mistake” always defeats willfulness without record support
Filing AOS without addressing prior visa fraud disclosed on forms

sections.heading: Sample language pointers
bullets: Separate: (1) whether ground applies; (2) waiver eligibility; (3) hardship; (4) discretion
Never coach clients to conceal prior misrepresentations

topics.title: False claim to U.S. citizenship
topics.practiceAreas: AOS | Removal | Naturalization | I-9 / benefits fraud

sections.heading: What this element requires
bullets: False representation of USC status on/after Sep 30, 1996 for any purpose/benefit under INA (incl. § 274A) or federal/state law
Can include: border claim, I-9 “USC” box, voter registration, some licenses
Generally no waiver for most applicants
Narrow statutory exception: both parents USC (or were), permanent U.S. residence before 16, reasonable belief of citizenship
Timely voluntary retraction may overcome in limited contexts; DOS may still discuss minor-capacity defenses — confirm current USCIS vs DOS policy

sections.heading: Facts that prove it
bullets: Exact claim → form/version, date, wording, who received it
Knowledge / capacity → age, advice received, language barriers (policy-sensitive)
Exception facts → parents’ citizenship; age at claim; residence history
Voting → separate unlawful voting deportability analysis

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
bullets: Treating as waivable misrepresentation under § 212(i)
Missing I-9 false USC claims during AOS/naturalization intake
Relying on outdated “knowing” / under-18 USCIS policy without checking current PM

sections.heading: Sample language pointers
bullets: Flag as strategy-critical / possibly fatal early
Distinguish misrepresentation (i) vs false claim (ii) in writing

sections.heading: What this element requires
bullets: Obtain certified dispositions — statute of conviction, sentence, date
Apply categorical / modified categorical approach before labeling CIMT or aggravated felony
Distinguish inadmissibility vs deportability criminal tests (they differ)
Controlled substances: broad § 212(a)(2)(A)(i)(II); deportability has ≤30g marijuana exception that may not help EWI/inadmissibility clients
§ 212(h) may waive some CIMTs / single ≤30g marijuana possession — check qualifying relatives / 15-year rehabilitation path; not available for many drug offenses

sections.heading: Facts that prove it
bullets: Court records → complaint, plea, judgment, sentence minutes
Record of conviction documents for divisible statutes
Rehabilitation → time since offense, counseling, employment
Immigration status at offense / entry mode (drives which INA section)

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
bullets: Guessing CIMT from charge title without elements analysis
Ignoring juvenile / vacated / expunged disposition rules (jurisdiction-specific)
Advising plea without Padilla-quality immigration screen
Assuming § 212(h) covers drug trafficking

sections.heading: Sample language pointers
bullets: “Record of conviction shows [statute]; elements analysis [pending / attorney].”
Mark `[CITE NEEDED]` for circuit-specific categorical holdings

sections.heading: What this element requires
bullets: Offense must match a § 101(a)(43) category after categorical analysis
Consequences often severe: deportability; asylum bar (AF = particularly serious for asylum); limited relief; permanent § 212(a)(9)(A) bar if removed as AF
Sentence length sometimes statutory (e.g., theft/crime of violence with ≥1 year) — suspended sentence may still “count” depending on category
Retroactivity and deportability-trigger dates can be circuit-sensitive — verify before advising

sections.heading: Facts that prove it
bullets: Exact statute + record of conviction
Imposed sentence / confinement
Date of conviction vs entry / adjustment / naturalization filing
Post-conviction relief status (vacatur grounds matter)

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
bullets: Equating any felony with aggravated felony
Missing state misdemeanors that still meet AF definitions via sentence
Advising asylum/cancellation without AF screen

sections.heading: Sample language pointers
bullets: State hypothesized (a)(43) subsection and why elements match/fail
Separate AF conclusion from CIMT / controlled-substance analysis

sections.heading: What this element requires
bullets: Refugee definition: past persecution or well-founded fear of future persecution
On account of protected ground: race, religion, nationality, particular social group, political opinion
Persecutor: government or private actor government unwilling/unable to control
Past persecution → presumption of future fear; DHS may rebut via changed circumstances or reasonable internal relocation
Credibility under totality (demeanor, consistency, plausibility) — REAL ID
One-year filing deadline unless changed/extraordinary circumstances + filing within reasonable time thereafter

sections.heading: Facts that prove it
bullets: Harm narrative → dates, actors, injuries, threats, detentions
Nexus → persecutor statements, pattern evidence, country conditions
PSG → immutable/fundamental trait, particularity, social distinction (circuit-sensitive)
Corroboration → medical, police reports, declarations, country reports
Timeline → U.S. arrival date; reasons for delayed filing

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
bullets: Conclusory PSG without particularity/social distinction
Ignoring one-year bar / exception proof
Inconsistencies across I-589, credible fear, and testimony
Treating withholding/CAT standards as identical to asylum

sections.heading: Sample language pointers
bullets: Structure: credibility → past harm → nexus → future fear → relocation → discretion
Cite country conditions exhibits by name/date

sections.heading: What this element requires
bullets: Screen bars early: persecutor; security danger; terrorist activity; particularly serious crime; serious nonpolitical crime abroad; firm resettlement (asylum)
Aggravated felony = particularly serious crime for asylum; for withholding, AF with ≥5-year sentence is particularly serious
Asylum is discretionary; withholding/CAT are mandatory if eligibility met (higher burden for withholding)
Firm resettlement bars asylum, not withholding
One-year deadline is a filing bar with limited exceptions

sections.heading: Facts that prove it
bullets: Criminal history → AF / PSC analysis
Third-country status → residence offers, permanent resettlement facts
Security / persecutor allegations → roles, timelines
Filing clock → arrival, status, trauma, counsel access

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
bullets: Stopping at asylum denial without evaluating withholding/CAT
Missing firm resettlement facts from prior safe-third residence
Assuming every AF bars withholding

sections.heading: Sample language pointers
bullets: Checklist bars before merits deep-dive
Explicitly state which protections remain if asylum is barred

sections.heading: What this element requires
bullets: Available in removal proceedings (not affirmative USCIS asylum office grants)
Withholding: clear probability (>50%) of persecution on a protected ground; mandatory if met and not barred
CAT: more likely than not torture by/with acquiescence of public official; no nexus to protected ground required
Neither is a path to LPR/citizenship; both can support work authorization
Bars differ from asylum (e.g., firm resettlement does not bar withholding; PSC thresholds differ)

sections.heading: Facts that prove it
bullets: Future risk evidence → country conditions, individualized threats
Torturer identity → government actor or acquiescence facts
Past torture/persecution as predictive evidence
Criminal bars screening → AF sentence length for withholding PSC

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
bullets: Using asylum “well-founded fear” burden language for withholding
Forgetting CAT when nexus is weak but government torture risk is strong
Promising green card pathway from withholding/CAT alone

sections.heading: Sample language pointers
bullets: State burden of proof explicitly for each form of protection
Separate nexus analysis (withholding) from CAT acquiescence analysis

sections.heading: What this element requires
bullets: Qualifying relationship + petitioner status (USC vs LPR)
Immediate relatives (IR): USC spouse; USC unmarried child <21; USC parent (petitioner ≥21) — no numerical quota
Preference: F1–F4 categories; subject to Visa Bulletin priority dates
Two-step: I-130 (or I-360) then AOS or consular immigrant visa
CSPA / surviving relative rules may preserve age or petition — screen when aging out or petitioner dies

sections.heading: Facts that prove it
bullets: Relationship docs → marriage, birth, adoption, termination of prior marriages
Petitioner status → naturalization cert, green card, passport
Priority date → I-130 receipt/approval; chart A vs B filing eligibility
Bona fides → for marriages, see `marriage-based-aos.md`

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
bullets: Filing AOS before priority date allows filing (wrong chart)
Missing prior marriage terminations
Assuming LPR petitioner can sponsor parent as IR (cannot)

sections.heading: Sample language pointers
bullets: State category + priority date + current bulletin chart used
Note derivative beneficiaries and aging-out risk

sections.heading: What this element requires
bullets: Bona fide marriage at inception (not solely for immigration)
Petitioner USC or LPR with qualifying status; IR if USC spouse
Conditional LPR if marriage <2 years at grant — later I-751 joint filing or waiver
Admissibility / waiver / discretion still required
Interview readiness: shared life facts, originals, consistent testimony

sections.heading: Facts that prove it
bullets: Bona fides → joint lease/mortgage, bank accounts, insurance, photos, messages, affidavits, children
Ceremony / license → civil marriage docs; prior divorce decrees
Cohabitation timeline → addresses since marriage
Abuse facts → if I-751 waiver / VAWA path

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
bullets: Thin bona fides packet for short courtship / large age gap / limited shared language
Filing without terminating prior marriages
Travel on advance parole without counseling on risks
Ignoring conditional residence clock

sections.heading: Sample language pointers
bullets: Organize exhibits by life domain (finances, residence, social, children)
Prepare couple for inconsistent secondary details vs core bona fides

topics.title: VAWA / U / T — humanitarian overview
topics.practiceAreas: VAWA | U visa | T visa | Humanitarian AOS

sections.heading: What this element requires
bullets: VAWA: battery/extreme cruelty by qualifying USC/LPR relative; good faith marriage if spouse path; residence with abuser (with exceptions); GMC; self-petition I-360 then AOS
U: qualifying criminal activity; substantial physical/mental abuse; helpfulness to law enforcement; admissible or waivable (broad U waivers)
T): severe form of trafficking; physically present on account of trafficking; compliance with reasonable LE requests (age/trauma exceptions); extreme hardship if removed
These paths often bypass standard I-130 petitioner control and some § 245(c) barriers — confirm case type

sections.heading: Facts that prove it
bullets: Abuse / crime / trafficking narrative + corroboration
Relationship / abuser status docs (VAWA)
LE certification I-918B / I-914B where required or strategic
Harm evidence → medical, mental health, police reports
Admissibility issues needing I-192 / other waivers

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
bullets: Forcing AOS through abuser-controlled I-130 when VAWA is safer
Missing derivative eligibility for children
Under-documenting helpfulness / LE contact for U

sections.heading: Sample language pointers
bullets: Safety planning first; never serve papers in ways that endanger client
Separate eligibility, waiver, and discretion sections

sections.heading: What this element requires
bullets: State whether client is: not in proceedings; NTA served but not filed; in IJ proceedings; BIA/appeal; post-order; reinstatement
Proceedings commence when NTA is filed with EOIR, not merely served
Identify charges: § 212 vs § 237; burden of proof flips accordingly
Note prior filings: I-485/I-589/I-130, denials, RFEs, motions, voluntary departure, prior orders
Reinstatement (§ 241(a)(5)) after unlawful reentry post-order sharply limits relief

sections.heading: Facts that prove it
bullets: NTA / OSC copies; EOIR case number; hearing notices
Prior orders → IJ/BIA/circuit; expedited removal
Receipt notices / FOIA / USCIS account history
Address history for in absentia / notice issues
ICE encounters / detainers / bond history

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
bullets: Filing AOS strategies without checking reinstatement / permanent bar
Missing that USCIS denial may still lead to NTA for priorities / asylum referrals
Confusing service of NTA with commencement

sections.heading: Sample language pointers
bullets: Open every strategy memo with a 3–5 line posture block
List pending forms + next hearing/action date

sections.heading: What this element requires
bullets: LPR cancellation (§ 240A(a)): LPR ≥5 years; continuous residence ≥7 years after lawful admission; not convicted of aggravated felony; discretion

Non-LPR cancellation (§ 240A(b)): continuous physical presence ≥10 years; GMC; not barred convictions; exceptional and extremely unusual hardship to USC/LPR spouse, parent, or child; discretion; annual caps
Stop-time rules for certain offenses / service of NTA — verify current Supreme Court / BIA rules before advising
Distinct from former § 212(c) (limited legacy cases only)

sections.heading: Facts that prove it
bullets: Admission / LPR card history; presence evidence (rent, school, medical, taxes)
Qualifying relative hardship (non-LPR) — elevated standard vs extreme hardship
Criminal matrix → AF / CIMT / stop-time triggers
Positive equities for discretion

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
bullets: Using ordinary extreme-hardship template for § 240A(b) (standard is higher)
Ignoring stop-time / presence breaks
Seeking cancellation when reinstatement / other bars apply

sections.heading: Sample language pointers
bullets: Label LPR vs non-LPR path in the first sentence
Hardship section must emphasize exceptional and extremely unusual for (b)

categories.title: Firm operations
categories.description: Intake, files, trust/billing, and calendaring checklists.

topics.title: Firm ops — intake checklist
topics.cite: Professional conduct (conflicts, competence, communication); Office Keeper Ch. 3 adapted for RMV immigration practice

sections.heading: What this element requires
bullets: Conflicts check before substantive consult (names, aliases, opposing parties, petitioning relatives, employers)
Capture immigration posture early: entries/exits, status, prior apps, criminal, fraud/USC claims
Identify goals + realistic pathways (AOS / consular / relief / not eligible)
Engagement letter / fee agreement signed; scope clear (what is / isn’t included)
Collect ID, status docs, prior receipts, court dispositions

sections.heading: Facts that prove it
bullets: Conflict search result saved to matter
Intake sheet: biographic, family tree, timeline, prior counsel
Signed retainer + fee schedule
Document request list with due dates

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
bullets: Starting work before conflict clearance
Missing criminal / false-claim questions that later sink AOS
Vague scope → disputes over appeals, RFEs, family derivatives

sections.heading: Sample language pointers
bullets: Use structured intake fields that map to assessment facts
End consult with written next-steps + document list

topics.title: Firm ops — file organization
topics.cite: Office Keeper Ch. 3–4 (file systems, naming, closing); adapt to AOD matter IDs

sections.heading: What this element requires
bullets: One matter ID = one digital file tree; avoid duplicate “working copies” outside CMS
Naming: `YYYY-MM-DD_doc-type_short-desc.ext` (or firm standard)
Subfolders: intake/, petitions/, evidence/, correspondence/, court/, billing/
Save email/PDFs into the matter — not only personal inboxes
Closing: final accounting, return/retain originals per policy, closing letter, retention schedule

sections.heading: Facts that prove it
bullets: Matter folder matches AOD matterId
Index of key filings with receipt numbers
Closing checklist completed + retention end date

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
bullets: Version chaos (“final_v7_REAL”)
Evidence only on staff laptop / WhatsApp
Closing without trust reconciliation

sections.heading: Sample language pointers
bullets: Prefer searchable filenames over nested deep trees
On close: “open items zero; trust balance zero; retention = [date]”

topics.title: Firm ops — trust & billing basics
topics.cite: RPC 1.15 (safekeeping); Office Keeper Ch. 2; jurisdiction-specific IOLTA rules (confirm local)

sections.heading: What this element requires
bullets: Separate operating vs client trust / IOLTA accounts
Unearned fees / advances in trust until earned; promptly transfer when earned and cleared
Client ledgers: receipts, disbursements, running balance; monthly three-way reconciliation
Retain trust records per jurisdictional period (Office Keeper example: 7 years — confirm local rule)
Written fee agreement; clear flat-fee vs hourly vs hybrid for immigration matters

sections.heading: Facts that prove it
bullets: Signed fee agreement
Trust ledger per matter
Monthly reconciliation reports
Invoices showing trust applications

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
bullets: Paying firm expenses directly from trust
Borrowing between client ledgers
Flat fees treated as earned before work/ethics rule allows
Ignoring unclaimed trust funds escheat rules

sections.heading: Sample language pointers
bullets: Invoice line: “Applied from trust” vs “Due from client”
Flag negative trust balance as emergency ethics issue

topics.title: Firm ops — calendaring & deadlines
topics.cite: Office Keeper Ch. 4 (calendaring / conflicts); EOIR / USCIS deadline practice

sections.heading: What this element requires
bullets: Dual calendaring: primary + backup for hard deadlines (RFE, appeal, IJ filing, biometrics, interview)
Immigration-critical dates: authorized stay end; UL presence thresholds; conditional residence / I-751 window; one-year asylum clock; NTA hearing
Conflict check integrated with new matter opening
Ticklers for receipt notices expected, FOIA follow-ups, Visa Bulletin checks

sections.heading: Facts that prove it
bullets: Calendar entries with matterId + responsible attorney
Deadline source document linked
Confirmation of backup calendar owner

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
bullets: Single-point-of-failure personal calendar only
Counting deadlines from wrong trigger (receipt vs decision vs service)
Missing derivative children’s aging-out dates

sections.heading: Sample language pointers
bullets: “Deadline = [date] / trigger = [event] / responsible = [name] / backup = [name]”
